sections.title: A step behind the story
sections.content: You know the *pluscuamperfecto* from B1 Unit 1: *había* plus a past participle, for something that had already happened before another moment in the past. In a story it does a special job. The story has its own "now", told with the *indefinido* and the *imperfecto*. The *pluscuamperfecto* steps behind that "now" to explain it: what had happened earlier and why things were the way they were.

sections.title: What a step back can do
rows: Estaba cansada porque no había dormido.
It explains the story's present: the cause lies one step further back.
Cuando llegué, ya se había ido.
It shows something that was already finished before an event of the story.
Nunca había visto un mar así.
It tells what the person had, or had not, experienced before this moment of the story.

items.spanish: Cuando llegó la ayuda, el fuego ya se había apagado.
items.english: When help arrived, the fire had already gone out.

items.spanish: Mi abuelo me había contado esa historia años antes, pero solo la recordé aquella noche.
items.english: My grandfather had told me that story years before, but I only remembered it that night.

items.spanish: Estaba nervioso porque nunca había hablado en público.
items.english: He was nervous because he had never spoken in public.

sections.content: In a longer flashback you do not need *había* in every sentence. Use the *pluscuamperfecto* to step back, then carry on in the *indefinido* and the *imperfecto*, and return to the *pluscuamperfecto* only if you need another step back: *Había salido de su pueblo a los veinte años. Primero trabajó en un hotel y después abrió una tienda.*
